title: Five who said yes
told: the history and tradition of Vaisakhi, 1699

hook.say: before the story, can i ask you something? have you ever been the first to stand up when nobody else would?
options: then you’ll understand daya ram. listen.
that’s okay. this one might help. listen.

steps.line: Vaisakhi, 1699. A huge crowd gathered at Anandpur for the spring harvest festival. Guru Gobind Singh raised a sword and asked: who will give their head for the faith?

steps.q: The crowd goes completely silent. What do you think happens?
steps.why: One man stood. Just one, at first.

steps.line: Silence. Then one man stood: Daya Ram, a shopkeeper from Lahore.
The Guru led him into a tent and came out alone. He asked again. What happened inside? The tellings differ.
Four more stood, one at a time: a farmer, a water-carrier, a cloth printer and a barber, from far corners of India.

steps.q: Why does it matter who the five were?
o: Each came from a different caste and region
They were the Guru’s closest relatives
They were the bravest soldiers present
steps.why: A shopkeeper, a farmer, a water-carrier, a printer, a barber. Their castes were kept apart. Now they stood together.

steps.q: The crowd waits outside the tent. What do you think happens?
o: The five are sent home quietly
The Guru comes out alone again
steps.why: All five walked out, alive and dressed alike, beside the Guru. Many tellings leave what happened in the tent a mystery.

steps.line: Then all five walked out alive, dressed alike, beside the Guru. Sikhs call them the Panj Pyare: the five beloved.

steps.q: Daya Ram’s first name means something. What?
steps.why: Daya is compassion. The others were Dharam (righteousness), Himmat (courage), Mohkam (firmness) and Sahib (master). Many Sikhs hear the five names as five virtues.

steps.line: They drank amrit, water and sugar stirred with a double-edged sword in one steel bowl. Then the Guru asked the five to give him amrit too.
Today, at Vaisakhi parades, five Sikhs dressed alike walk at the front. They stand in for those five.
steps.label: today

steps.q: Five people still lead every amrit ceremony today. Who can they be?
o: The five eldest in the room
steps.why: Any five Sikhs who keep the faith fully can stand as the Panj Pyare. Sikhism has no priestly caste: the five stand in for the whole community.

say: here’s what i love. five strangers stood up when nobody else would, and walked out as one family.
sikhs call that family the khalsa. men take the name singh, lion, and women kaur, princess. names in place of caste.

steps.q: After the five, the Guru asked them to give him amrit too. What does that show?
o: The five now outranked the Guru
The Guru joined them as an equal
The amrit only works from five hands
steps.why: The teacher became the student. Sikh tradition puts it simply: the Guru became the disciple.

today.say: the five came from homes that never shared a meal, and drank from one bowl. today, share food or a drink with someone outside your usual circle, like family.
options: then that’s your yes for today.
good. the five were strangers too.

card.keepWhy: Five strangers, one bowl, one family.
sources: Vaisakhi 1699 at Anandpur Sahib: Guru Gobind Singh’s call for a head and the founding of the Khalsa (traditional accounts; Sikh Rehat Maryada on Amrit)
The Panj Pyare: Bhai Daya Singh (Lahore), Bhai Dharam Singh (Hastinapur, near Delhi), Bhai Himmat Singh (Jagannath Puri), Bhai Mohkam Singh (Dwarka), Bhai Sahib Singh (Bidar)
The Guru receiving amrit from the five, “aape gur chela” (the Guru is himself the disciple), Bhai Gurdas II, Vaar 41
